strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G) with state-of-the-art performance among 3B models; particularly impressive data efficiency with only 85k screenshots versus millions used by baselines

Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablation studies (Table 4) that justify each component, convergence analysis showing faster training than baselines, and detailed analysis of the two-step inference strategy

Well-motivated technical design: the <ANCHOR> token elegantly separates GUI grounding from general language understanding, avoiding harmful direct supervision on query tokens; overlap- and center-aware labeling aligns with human clicking behavior
Technically sound methodology with correct mathematics and fair experimental setup; careful ablations control for confounding factors using a fixed 45k dataset for baseline comparisons

Practical advantages: coordinate-free formulation naturally supports post-hoc zoom-in refinement without retraining, valuable for real deployments on variable-resolution screens; no additional modules compared to GUI-Actor
Clear presentation with effective figures (especially Figures 2-3) communicating complex multi-head aggregation logic; generally well-organized writing
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core idea of using attention for GUI grounding is established (TAG, GUI-Actor); contributions are primarily engineering-focused, with <ANCHOR> token being a straightforward simplification and overlap-aware labeling borrowed from GUI-G2

Visual-sink query token mechanism lacks strong theoretical justification: using hidden state similarity (Eq. 7) over attention-based measures is weakly motivated; claims about 'semantic heads' rely on citations rather than empirical validation within this work; global uniform Qs (Eq. 9) vs. layer-wise (Eq. 10) shows only marginal ablation differences

Confounded performance evaluation: main result (58.6% on ScreenSpot-Pro) includes zoom-in refinement, making it difficult to isolate core method contribution; base method achieves only 45.2%, and improvements without zoom-in are modest (0.4% on ScreenSpot-v2 versus GUI-Actor-3B)

Ambiguous presentation of variants: both soft (Eq. 11) and hard (Eq. 8) weighting schemes presented without clear guidance on when to use which; soft variant outperforms base on ScreenSpot-Pro but not ScreenSpot-v2, suggesting the hard topK selection may be suboptimal

Narrow scope and limited generalization: evaluation restricted to single-region GUI grounding; generalization to other MLLM backbones untested (only Qwen2.5-VL-3B evaluated); no multi-region grounding despite potential; insights unlikely to transfer beyond GUI grounding

Reproducibility and methodological concerns: no code release mentioned, project page URL missing; no error bars or significance testing provided; single-run results without variance across seeds; modest improvements (e.g., 1.26% from weighted labeling) lack statistical validation

Incomplete error analysis and ablation: no discussion of failure modes or when method struggles; zoom-in strategy treats offset errors as symptom rather than addressing root causes; hyperparameter choices (α=0.8, topK=1) lack sensitivity analysis; soft vs. hard variant sensitivity not explored

Presentation clarity issues: abstract claims 58.6% without mentioning zoom-in, potentially misleading; multiple anchor token variants in appendix (anchor_start, anchor, anchor_end) versus simplified main-text description; two-variant naming creates confusion about main contribution

Baseline comparison fairness: most results from original papers with different training data and hyperparameters; GUI-Actor comparison on 45k ablation dataset shows marginal ScreenSpot-v2 improvement (0.4%); mixed scaling comparisons (3B vs. 7B/72B) make method contribution unclear

strengths: Strong empirical results with exceptional data efficiency: achieves competitive performance with only 85k training images versus millions for baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks with thorough ablation studies systematically validating each design component
Clear practical motivation mirroring human behavior: selecting relevant regions first, then determining precise location within patches
Demonstrates faster training convergence than vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor, supporting claimed efficiency gains
Practical two-step zoom-in inference mechanism requires no additional training and provides meaningful performance improvements
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core ideas (attention-based grounding from TAG, coordinate-free approach from GUI-Actor) are incremental refinements rather than novel contributions; weighted patch labeling directly borrowed from GUI-G2

Visual-sink query token selection lacks rigor: justification relies on citations about 'semantic heads' without establishing relevance for GUI grounding; Appendix A analysis (Figure 5) shows only marginal differences between embedding and attention correlations; choice of top-1 is ad-hoc without principled justification

Incomplete justification of core assumptions: paper never verifies that <ANCHOR> token truly captures all query token information; claim that query token attention supervision impairs capabilities contradicts the vanilla attention grounding approach which also supervises attention directly

Experimental fairness concerns: GUI-Actor comparison on identical 45k subset shows modest improvements (2.12% on ScreenSpot-v2, 7.40% on ScreenSpot-Pro); inconsistent performance across variants (soft matching excels on ScreenSpot-Pro but underperforms on v2) without clear guidance for practitioners

Reproducibility and generalization issues: no code/model release mentioned; single backbone evaluation (Qwen2.5-VL-3B only) limits understanding of generalization; hyperparameter choices (α=0.8, top-K=1, crop size) appear ad-hoc without sensitivity analysis

Post-hoc engineering concerns: zoom-in strategy addresses offset error symptoms rather than root causes; Table 5 shows 33-48 predictions degrade after second step, indicating lack of robustness; unclear whether improvements come from base model or zoom-in alone
Confusing dual variants: paper presents two competing variants (visual-sink vs soft KL-matching) with trade-offs not explained; no principled recommendation for which to use

Weak performance on abstract visual elements: icon accuracy only 24.2% on ScreenSpot-Pro versus 61.6% for text, suggesting method struggles with non-textual UI elements; limited analysis of failure cases

strengths: Strong empirical results across three benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G) with exceptional data efficiency (85k images vs. millions for competitors)
Clever algorithmic design with learnable <ANCHOR> token for efficient attention aggregation and visual-sink query selection for principled head weighting
Thorough ablation studies (Table 4) systematically validating each component with convergence analysis and controlled experiments on 45k subset
Practical advantages: no warm-up training required, fastest convergence, and plug-and-play zoom-in mechanism without additional training
Outperforms much larger models on key benchmarks (e.g., UI-TARS-7B on ScreenSpot-v2: 91.6% vs. 90.8%)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figs. 2-3) and sufficient implementation details for reproducibility
Methodologically rigorous analysis of offset errors (Table 5) and performance breakdown by task category
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily an engineering improvement over prior attention-based grounding (TAG, vanilla attention grounding); <ANCHOR> token is a straightforward simplification

Visual-sink query token mechanism lacks rigorous justification: the argument that semantic heads show consistent patterns in hidden states (vs. attention) is hand-wavy; relegated to appendix; why top-K=1 consistently outperforms K=2,3 is unexplained and suggests over-optimization

Inconsistent presentation of variants: GUI-AIMA-3B (soft) performs better on ScreenSpot-Pro but worse on ScreenSpot-v2, with no principled guidance on variant selection; soft pattern matching (Eq. 11) feels ad-hoc
Performance not definitively state-of-the-art: UI-TARS-1.5-7B achieves 64.2% on OSWorld-G vs. 62.2% for GUI-AIMA-3B + zoom-in; inconsistent improvements on fine-grained manipulation tasks
Incomplete analysis: no discussion of failure modes, non-English GUIs, or sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., why α=0.8?); limited scope (single-region only)
Hybrid loss design (next-token + attention loss) obscures the isolated contribution of the proposed attention alignment
Reproducibility concerns: no code/model release mentioned; sparse dataset sampling details; arbitrary hyperparameter choices lack justification

strengths: Well-motivated and elegantly designed anchor token mechanism that cleanly solves the problem of query token aggregation without impractical explicit weighting
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 benchmarks with state-of-the-art results among 3B models (61.5% ScreenSpot-Pro, 92.1% ScreenSpot-v2) demonstrating strong empirical performance
Thorough ablation studies (Table 5) clearly validating each design choice: anchor tokens (1.50-4.24% improvement), visual-sink selection (1.90% improvement), patch-wise labeling (1.26% improvement)
Impressive data efficiency with only 509k training samples (~101k screenshots), showing faster convergence than GUI-Actor and requiring no warm-up stage
Detailed analysis of design contributions including head weight visualization (Figure 6), zoom-in effectiveness (Table 6: 31% error reduction), and attention head pruning experiments
Practical two-step zoom-in inference procedure that requires no additional training and naturally extends the patch-based formulation
Clear presentation with effective use of figures and tables; methodology section is well-organized and technical details properly documented
weaknesses: Limited novelty: coordinate-free attention-based grounding already explored in TAG (Xu et al., 2024a); core contribution is improved aggregation via anchor tokens and visual-sink head weighting, which is incremental rather than conceptually new

Confounded contribution attribution: the 7.7% improvement on ScreenSpot-Pro (53.8%→61.5%) substantially derives from the orthogonal zoom-in stage rather than the core attentional mechanism, making it difficult to isolate the actual method's contribution

Data efficiency claims lack proper qualification: GUI-AIMA-3B uses 250k samples from GroundCUA (in-domain for UI-Vision); comparisons with models trained on different data distributions (e.g., GUI-Actor on 9.6M) require more careful framing

Significant performance gaps remain unaddressed: icon grounding is substantially weaker than text (47.9% vs 70.0% on ScreenSpot-Pro+zoom); fine-grained manipulation weak (48.7% on OSWorld-G+zoom); no failure analysis or explanation for these limitations
Missing reproducibility elements: project page URL is blank; no code release mentioned; GroundCUA dataset availability unclear; these gaps hinder reproducibility despite detailed methods

Absent discussion of limitations and societal impact: no failure case analysis, no discussion of single-region limitation, no ethical considerations for GUI automation; especially important given autonomous agent applications

Visual-sink token selection lacks theoretical justification: the concept is empirically motivated but the explanation for why hidden-state similarity outperforms attention relies on general transformer literature rather than task-specific reasoning; layer-wise vs. global trade-off (Table 5 shows layer-wise slightly better on icons) not adequately justified

Dense technical presentation: visual-sink token concept introduced abruptly; transition from Eq. (1) vanilla to Eq. (2) simplified aggregation could be clearer; interpretation of attention weight patterns (Figure 6) is limited

Strong empirical results competitive with larger models (7B, 30B) while maintaining 3B scale
Thorough ablation studies systematically validating each component
Well-motivated shift from coordinate-based to attention-based patch-level grounding
Practical two-step zoom-in inference requiring no additional training
Faster convergence compared to GUI-Actor and vanilla attention grounding
Clear presentation with informative visualizations of methodology

strengths: Strong empirical results across 5 diverse GUI grounding benchmarks (61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 92.1% on ScreenSpot-v2, 68.1% on OSWorld-G) with only ~101k screenshots, demonstrating notable data efficiency compared to competitors using millions of examples

Well-motivated coordinate-free formulation that addresses limitations of text-based coordinate generation by directly supervising attention maps, providing more intuitive alignment with visual grounding

Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablations (Table 5), convergence analysis (Fig. 5), two-step inference analysis (Table 6), and attention head contribution visualization (Fig. 6)

Practical advantages: no additional modules needed, single-stage training without warm-up, two-step zoom-in inference works without retraining, and efficient attention extraction with minimal overhead

Clear technical design with complementary components: <ANCHOR> token elegantly sidesteps token-wise weight calibration, and visual-sink token selection provides head-agnostic signal for identifying grounding-relevant attention heads
Consistent improvements across different domains (desktop, mobile, web) and competitive performance with substantially larger models despite 3B parameters
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: individual components (appended <ANCHOR> token, top-K similarity-based token selection, overlap-aware patch labeling) are relatively straightforward; novelty lies primarily in careful combination rather than fundamental innovations

Incomplete justification for key design choices: hidden-state similarity (Eq. 4) is claimed superior to attention for selecting visual-sink tokens but lacks rigorous empirical validation; hyperparameters (α=0.8, crop 616px, 2× zoom) lack ablation studies

Ad-hoc two-step zoom-in strategy, while effective, appears task-specific and orthogonal to main contribution; Table 6 shows it corrects 215 predictions but loses 33 originally-correct ones; generalization to other domains unclear
Training data heterogeneity: GUI-AIMA-3B uses additional 250k GroundCUA instructions not used by all baselines, complicating fair comparison between variants and across methods
Missing analysis of failure modes, error characterization, and challenging GUI task types; no discussion of patch-level supervision limitations (small targets, overlapping elements)
Modest practical efficiency gains in practice: ~26% training time improvement but nearly identical inference time (0.76 vs 0.73 s/iteration); efficiency claims somewhat oversold
Framework limited to single-region grounding with multi-region grounding deferred to future work; unclear if insights generalize beyond GUI tasks to broader visual grounding problems

No statistical rigor: lacks confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; some performance differences marginal (e.g., ScreenSpot-v2: 92.1% vs 91.5%); single-epoch training may indicate high variance
